canberra.title: Powered-up Williamsdale battery plugged-in, with more to come
canberra.snippet: The “big battery” at Williamsdale, now sending energy into the electricity grid, won’t be the last for the ACT. Governm...
canberra.content:
The new Williamsdale BESS is part of a renewable energy hub, with the solar farm next door. Photo: Eku.

The “big battery” at Williamsdale, now sending energy into the electricity grid, won’t be the last for the ACT.

Government and company officials gathered on site on Thursday (5 November) for a ceremony to mark the commissioning of Eku Energy’s 250 mW Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) after a two-year build.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr said a growing population, the shift away from gas to electric appliances, electric vehicle take-up and a warming climate all meant demand for electricity would also increase.

Mr Barr said Canberra was electrifying faster than any other place in the country, and it needed an energy system that met that challenge and was reliable, resilient and capable of supporting Canberra’s next stage of growth.

“This battery helps deliver exactly that,” he said.

“It provides Canberra with a substantial reserve of stored energy, strengthens the electricity network, and helps ensure that renewable energy generated here in the ACT and elsewhere is available when it is needed most in our energy market.”

Mr Barr said that, like previous generations, today’s generation had a responsibility to invest in the infrastructure that would support a sustainable future, by “not simply meeting today’s needs, but preparing for tomorrow’s opportunities”.

Part of the Canberra Big Battery network being established across Canberra, the Williamsdale BESS was an important project for the Territory, Mr Barr said.

“But I don’t think it’ll be the last major renewable energy storage site, nor will it be the last entity that’s trading in the national energy market as well,” he said.

Mr Barr believed there was still plenty of room in the ACT and beyond to accommodate such infrastructure.

The BESS switch-on comes amid ongoing debate in the regions about renewable energy development and the appropriateness of sites, including the giant Flat Rock proposal on Uriarra Station in the west of the ACT.

Mr Barr said Williamsdale, where a solar farm was already operating and transmission lines were nearby, was appropriate.

He said governments and proponents needed to be sensitive to community concerns and earn a social licence for such developments.

Power for a third of Canberra for two hours during peak demand periods. Photos: Ian Bushnell.

Eku's Elias Saba, Tom Best, Brindabella MLA Taimus Werner-Gibbings, and Chief Minister Andrew Barr.

Eku Chief Operating Officer Tom Best said his company took an open-book approach.

“We’re not trying to push approvals through without everybody being aware of what we’re doing and the infrastructure that we’re looking to build,” he said.

He was not frustrated by the ongoing debate but said Australia needed to get on with the energy transition.

“Everybody has a view, and I think we have to be open to hearing those and responding to them in the right way,” he said.

But “there’s an absolute risk to energy security going forward if we don’t start to work further into the transition”.

The Williamsdale BESS can store enough electricity to power one-third of Canberra for two hours during peak demand periods, and will support the ACT electricity network, strengthening energy security and reliability for the ACT and NSW.

The system can also respond to grid changes within milliseconds, storing renewable energy and making it available when it is needed most. This will strengthen the reliability and resilience of Canberra’s energy system, especially during periods of high demand.

The facility includes 136 Tesla Megapacks 2 batteries arranged in 12 collector grids, each with 12 step-up transformers. The batteries are connected to the electricity network through a main transformer that is larger than an ACTION bus and weighs over 180 tonnes.

It was delivered through an Australia-first, 15-year revenue-sharing model in which the government had no upfront costs for the development and will receive an expected $20-25 million a year from revenue generated by the BESS’s participation in the National Electricity Market.

In return, the government will make a quarterly payment to Eku.

Mr Best said Eku hoped the Williamsdale BESS would be remembered as a project that demonstrated the power of collaboration – “a project that brought together the government, the industry, researchers, communities and local organisations behind a shared goal”.

Eku has distributed $1,000,000 in community benefits grants to local not-for-profit groups and the Centre for Energy Systems at the Australian National University to further their research into the most suitable energy system for the ACT.

Mr Barr said the Canberra Big Battery, along with smaller neighbourhood batteries, would play a big role in the ACT’s transition to net zero emissions by 2045.

canberra.title: Exclusive Canberra women’s club caught in geopolitical crossfire
canberra.snippet: An exclusive Canberra club has been dragged into a murky geopolitical storm after the wives of several ambassadors withdrew their members...
canberra.content:
The Women’s International Club of Canberra invites members who are newcomers to Canberra, in particular diplomats, their families, and embassy staff. Photo: WIC.

An exclusive Canberra club has been dragged into a murky geopolitical storm after the wives of several ambassadors withdrew their membership.

POLITICO reported on 3 November that the Women’s International Club of Canberra (WIC) recently admitted the wife of Russia’s ambassador to Australia, Irina Petrakova. As a result, the wives of the ambassadors of Ukraine, Italy and Estonia have withdrawn their memberships.

The WIC describes itself as a club of more than 300 women from 50 countries who enjoy Canberra and what it has to offer.

It says newcomers to Canberra – in particular diplomats, their families, and embassy staff – are invited to join and “warmly welcomed” to the club. Australian and permanent residents of Canberra are also welcomed, but must be invited by a current member.

The membership has interest groups known as circles that participate in activities such as bridge, mahjong, tennis, walking, book and language groups, craft groups, dining, photography, meditation, origami, aikido and other activities.

The report says the president of WIC Sandie Kaine said the club had admitted Mrs Petrakova after it received legal advice that it would be discriminatory to refuse her membership because of her country of origin.

“The Russian Ambassador’s spouse was admitted to WIC in accordance with the law and the WIC Constitution,” she said in a statement.

Russian Ambassador to Australia Mikhail Petrakov (left) with his wife Irina Petrakova (right) presented his credentials to Governor-General Sam Mostyn in September 2025. Photo: Russian Embassy.

But Liana Myroshnychenko – whose husband Vasyl is Ukraine’s Ambassador to Australia and New Zealand – informed the club’s membership that her objection to Mrs Petrakova’s membership was as a representative of Russia, not her nationality.

Russia conducted a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 after occupying the Ukrainian territories of Crimea and Donbas since 2014. In 2023, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued arrest warrants for a number of Russia’s leaders including President Vladimir Putin over alleged war crimes in Ukraine, including the alleged kidnapping of tens of thousand of children, attacks on civilian infrastructure, and unlawful killing of civilians.

Russia has rejected the ICC’s charges, and says the body has no legal jurisdiction over Russian citizens or heads of state.

Russia has also threatened other European nations, has repeatedly violated Estonian, Finnish, Polish, Danish, and German airspace using drones, and has been accused of using ‘grey zone’ warfare tactics against Baltic and EU states in the form of cyber-attacks and interfering with undersea cables and energy pipelines.

European Union (EU) ambassador to Australia Lawrence Meredith told POLITICO the EU was “deeply disappointed” by the WIC’s admission of Mrs Petrakova, saying, “The EU can accept no normalisation of Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine, whatsoever”.

In a 4 November LinkedIn post, Ambassador Myroshnychenko said Mrs Petrakova “represents a Russia that kills, maims, commits sexual violence and subjects people to horrific torture – a Russia for which, through its actions, the value of human life appears to be disregarded”.

He said this included the lives of 283 passengers, including 38 Australians, who were on board Malaysia Airlines MH17, which was shot down by Russian-backed forces over Ukraine in July 2014.

“As my beloved wife Liana has rightly put it in the resignation letter: ‘This is not about a Russian woman simply because she is Russian,’ but because she is in Australia representing ‘the country that killed my cousin, burned my friend alive, took the lives of many of my friends from school and university.’”

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: Health care and social work lead slow growth in public sector jobs
canberra.snippet: Growth in public sector jobs across Australia is at its lowest since the COVID pandemic, and wage growth last year was lower than the pre...
canberra.content:
Growth in public sector jobs is at its lowest since COVID, with state-based health care and social care employment leading what growth there is. Photo: YuriArcursPeopleimages.

Growth in public sector jobs across Australia is at its lowest since the COVID pandemic, and wage growth last year was lower than the previous one.

Public sector jobs across the nation rose 2.3 per cent over the past financial year, and wages increased 6.6 per cent over the same 12-month period, according to the latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

Between June 2025 and June 2026, health care and social work led the employment bump for public sector jobs, followed by roles in education and training.

Employment growth was led by state and territory government public sectors.

ABS head of labour statistics Sean Crick said wages paid to public sector employees totalled $266.1 billion across all levels of government in 2025-26.

“This was an increase of 6.6 per cent, down from the 7.8 per cent annual growth recorded in 2024-25.

“The moderation in wage growth in 2025-26 reflected slowing growth in Commonwealth and local government jobs.

“The 2.3 per cent annual increase in total public sector jobs was the slowest since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2019-20.”

The ABS’s figures for the public sector are concentrated in three key industries: public administration and safety; education and training; and health care and social assistance.

Together, these three industries account for nearly 90 per cent of public sector jobs and wages.

“Growth in the 2025-26 public sector wage bill was driven by a combination of underlying wage growth and ongoing demand for health and education services within state and territory governments,” Mr Crick said.

“Of [the] three industries, health care and social assistance recorded the strongest rate of growth in 2025-26 for both jobs and wages.”

Health care and social assistance jobs rose by 29,700 (+4.4 per cent) to 669,800 between June 2025 and June 2026. Wages paid increased by $5.5 billion (+8.5 per cent) to $70.9 billion in 2025-26.

Education and training jobs increased by 17,400 (+2.3 per cent) to 790,800, while wages paid rose by $3.2 billion (+5.2 per cent) to $64.6 billion.

Public administration and safety jobs increased by 4600 (+0.5 per cent) to 883,300, while wages paid rose by $5.6 billion (+6.2 per cent) to $96.5 billion.

The ABS has also responded to public and policy interest in artificial intelligence (AI) and its impact on the overall Australian labour market by adding new questions to the quarterly Job Vacancies Survey.

The questions aim to capture the potential relationship between AI and job vacancies, both now and in the next 12 months.

Data collected so far shows AI has had a limited impact on job vacancies.

“About 82 per cent of businesses reported that AI did not impact the level of job vacancies in August 2026,” Mr Crick said.

“Four per cent of businesses reported that AI had reduced the number of job vacancies in August, while less than one per cent reported that AI had led to an increase in vacancies in their business.”

However, the impact of AI on job vacancies differed across industries, with the information media and telecommunications category seeing the highest proportion of businesses reporting a 16 per cent decrease in vacancies due to AI.

This was followed by the wholesale trade sector, down 8 per cent, and manufacturing, down 6 per cent.

The industries with the highest proportions of businesses reporting an increase in vacancies due to AI were electricity, gas, water and waste services (10 per cent), public administration and safety (4 per cent) and health care and social assistance (2 per cent).

The ABS also asked businesses about the expected impact of AI on job vacancies in their business over the next 12 months.

“About two-thirds of businesses said that they did not expect AI to impact their job vacancies over the next 12 months,” Mr Crick said.

“About 8 per cent of businesses expected that AI will lead to a decrease in job vacancies and one per cent expected it would lead to an increase.”

canberra.title: ‘No, I didn’t phone you’: Telstra explains mystery calls amid network complaints
canberra.snippet: Last night, three people phoned me saying they were returning my call. The problem? I hadn’t called any of them. And it seems I was...
canberra.content:
5 November 2026

Join the conversation

1

Telstra customers were left confused over missed calls last night. Photo: Region.

Last night, three people phoned me saying they were returning my call.

The problem? I hadn’t called any of them.

And it seems I wasn’t alone, with Telstra customers across Australia suddenly receiving mysterious missed call and voicemail notifications, despite their phones never ringing.

The bizarre episode comes amid broader concerns about Telstra’s regional network, with customers in parts of the Riverina and NSW South Coast also reporting connectivity problems.

Telstra has now admitted a technical glitch was behind the mystery calls episode, blaming a problem with its MessageBank service.

A Telstra spokesperson said the issue had been identified and fixed on Wednesday night (4 November), but warned some customers might have received a backlog of missed call and voicemail notifications at once.

“Some customers may have noticed several delayed missed call and voicemail notifications arriving at once, some dating back to several days,” the spokesperson said.

“We’re sorry for the confusion this may have caused.”

Importantly, Telstra said there had been no impact to triple zero calls, ordinary voice calls or mobile data.

The incident has also renewed scrutiny of Telstra’s network reliability, following a major nationwide outage in July which disrupted mobile services and left hundreds of triple zero calls unable to connect.

An independent investigation into that outage later identified problems with the way Telstra managed its network timing systems.

Meanwhile, questions remain about the quality of Telstra’s regional network, with customers reporting internet dropouts, slow connections and other service problems in parts of the Riverina and along the NSW South Coast, including Griffith and Batemans Bay.

Asked about the complaints, Telstra said its local team had advised that both regions covered a large number of mobile sites.

“We continuously monitor the performance of our mobile network and respond to issues as they arise,” the spokesperson said.

The company said it would provide advice later today about issues in Griffith and Batemans Bay in particular.

More to come.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: WATCH: E-scooter rider caught overtaking car on Southern Cross Drive
canberra.snippet: Canberrans have been left stunned by a video of an e-scooter rider exceeding the 60 km/h speed limit down Southern Cross Drive. Local Gra...
canberra.content:
5 November 2026

Southern Cross Drive has a 60 km/h speed limit, but this e-scooter rider was clearly going faster. Photo: Graham Pryce/Facebook.

Canberrans have been left stunned by a video of an e-scooter rider exceeding the 60 km/h speed limit down Southern Cross Drive.

Local Graham Pryce posted the incident on Facebook, expressing his shock at being overtaken by the rider.

“What’s he doing there, about 80?” he’s heard asking his passenger.

“At least go on the footpath, bro.”

His passenger can be heard stating, “That’s just a disaster waiting to happen”.

E-scooters are classified as personal mobility devices in the ACT and are only allowed to be used in public spaces if they have a maximum speed of 25 km/h “on level ground”.

The ACT Government’s City Services information page stated that if a private e-scooter doesn’t meet all requirements (including the imposed speed limit), it’s not allowed on public roads or paths.

“It may only be used on private property,” it stated.

“Any personal mobility device that travels more than 25 km/h is considered a motor vehicle and is therefore forbidden from travelling on paths.”

It is illegal in the ACT to ride an e-scooter faster than 15 km/h on footpaths, or faster than 25 km/h on shared paths, bicycle paths or the bicycle side of separated paths.

There are special circumstances for e-scooters to be ridden on roads.

This applies when there’s no footpath, shared path or nature strip next to the road or when it’s not practical or safe to use such alternatives.

“If you must travel on a road, take the shortest practical route and return to an approved path as soon as possible. Do not stay on the road for longer than necessary,” City Services advised.

“If you are using an e-scooter or other personal mobility device, you must stick to the speed limits.”

Canberra Escooter Club president David Hine wants police to crack down on illegal rider behaviour.

“The e-scooter in the video has had its speed limiter disabled,” he said.

“Many scooters can reach 100 km/h.”

He felt most private riders were aware of Canberra’s 25 km/h speed limit, and pointed to NSW and QLD’s e-scooter and e-bike campaigns as successful ways to deter illegal behaviour.

ACT Policing can’t provide statistics on e-scooter cases as it doesn’t differentiate between privately owned and rideshare e-scooters.

Officer in Charge of Road Policing Detective Inspector Mark Steel said poor behaviour by e-scooter riders was a concern, especially when incidents could result in “significant” injuries.

“E-scooter riders are vulnerable road users because they are not afforded the same protections as someone who is travelling in a vehicle and are at a higher risk of death or serious injury in the event of a collision,” they said.

Police officers can issue fines to any e-scooter rider who’s found to be breaking the law.

This includes not wearing a helmet, travelling on the road, riding with another person, and using a mobile phone while riding.

Road offences and dashcam footage can be reported to ACT Policing through its online portal.

australia.title: David Jones wrongly believed it could be exclusive and everywhere. Can the 188-year-old institution keep the lights on for Christmas?
australia.snippet: The arbiter of Australian taste abandoned prestige to chase profits through expansion. Now 6,000 staff across 38 stores fear job cuts as ...
australia.content:
I cut past the glow of the Louis Vuitton displays and sidestep Armani, Hermès and Prada, all while being hit by the mingling fragrances on the ground level at David Jones.

A series of escalators at the heart of its flagship Sydney store carries me to the menswear department, where I’m greeted by Ralph Lauren and Tommy Hilfiger.

I see signs promoting a price match, a concession made after David Jones followed mass-market retailers into the suburbs and began stocking the same products shoppers can find elsewhere.

The arbiter of Australian taste abandoned prestige for size, after wrongly believing it could be both exclusive and everywhere.

Now the 188-year-old has collapsed into administration after it fell behind on rent, and emergency talks between the David Jones owner, Anchorage Capital, and lenders and landlords unravelled.

The receivers FTI Consulting, which has taken over operational control as the business gets prepped for sale, has issued an ominous warning that “difficult decisions” must be made.

About 6,000 staff spread across a network of 38 stores face uncertain job prospects, not knowing how long the department store will be able to keep its doors open and Christmas-light displays on.

Some of the most unprofitable stores – typically in outer suburban and regional locations – are at risk of imminent closure.

The way back, according to retail experts, is a radical retreat to a tight network of premium stores in prime locations, which would involve cutting the number of stores.

While that reimagined footprint could save the business, it will hinge on an uncertain administration process whereby different stakeholders vie to protect their interests.

“If it survives this, in five years or so, it wouldn’t surprise me to see 12 to 15 David Jones stores,” says Retail Doctor Group’s chief executive, Brian Walker.

“A smaller, reimagined business could be quite profitable.”

Scaling exclusivity

Many retailers have been through a torrid decade, with online buying habits ushered in by Amazon proving to be an existential threat to department stores around the world.

Retailers like David Jones, however, were supposed to be immune because they were seen as high-end shopping destinations that could not be replaced by online carts.

That confidence proved misplaced, with similar-era peers including Lord & Taylor in the US having already succumbed.

David Jones has cycled through almost every type of ownership model, from public listing to foreign conglomerate ownership and now private equity, with most of those models favouring profit through expansion.

But there is an uncomfortable question as to whether an institution built on exclusivity was ever designed to be scaled across suburban shopping centres.

Walker says the distress at David Jones has been caused by its large lease commitments at under-performing sites.

“Suddenly David Jones was trying to appeal to the mass market to keep this machine fed by mirroring the growth of shopping centres into the suburbs,” he says.

“The store network needs to recalibrate.”

The receivers will want to keep David Jones trading through the Black Friday and Christmas rush, a critical period when customers will inject desperately needed cash into the store network, as administrators search for a buyer.

The process could provide an avenue to shed lease commitments at unprofitable stores and push through widespread job cuts.

‘Death by a thousand cuts’

Many Australians have a view on what type of customer service they expect at David Jones, with some longing for the white-glove service of a past era.

The RMIT University advertising professor Robert Crawford says there can be a clash between a customer’s memory of what it was like to go to David Jones decades ago and the reality on the shop floor.

“For a business model that established service as a key part of its unique selling proposition, when you go in there and don’t get that, people are getting understandably annoyed, and this hasn’t just appeared overnight,” Crawford says.

“It’s been a bit of a death by a thousand cuts.”

Part of the awkwardness is that David Jones now resembles what some analysts describe as “generalist luxury”, a segment of the market where customers are not certain what type of service, or product exclusivity, they should expect.

For example, in 1948, David Jones hosted an in-store Christian Dior parade, which was the first collection of the French fashion designer shown outside Paris. Now, those brands have their own standalone stores, and several have removed some of their premier products from David Jones.

Well away from the ground-floor glow of designer bags and imported fragrances, the store settles into decor that is pleasant enough but is not a destination.

I sit near Polo Ralph Lauren sneakers and Birkenstocks in the men’s department at the Elizabeth Street store on a quiet Monday morning, three days before the collapse into administration.

The service is polite and unhurried but there are few shoppers demanding attention.

A sign advertises the store’s complimentary styling and fitting services for men’s clothing. I check online and the next available appointment at this flagship store is at 2pm. In two weeks’ time.

It is indicative of a retailer caught between the luxury of its past and the financial pressures of its present; an old institution offering personal service – so long as you can wait a fortnight to be measured.

australia.title: Victorian election: high costs and unkept promises could flip Melbourne’s Labor heartland to One Nation
australia.snippet: Labor ignored its falling vote in the working-class western suburbs because they would never go Liberal – but now there’s another option ...
australia.content:
It’s nearing 3pm outside Beirut Bakehouse, a Lebanese bakery tucked inside a shopping plaza in Taylors Lakes, 20km north-west of Melbourne. A group of men are out the front nursing coffees and smoking cigarettes, in what appears to be a regular gathering.

But despite their closeness, three of the group will be casting their votes for three different political parties in next month’s state election.

Brian, a retired businessman, is leaning Liberal. Ivan says he’s going to give One Nation a go. Antonio, a lifelong Labor voter, is sticking with the party – though he understands why others aren’t.

“They’re all working class here and that’s basically what Labor is,” Antonio says.

“But I suppose they feel abandoned.”

The men are enrolled in Sydenham – one of several Labor seats in Melbourne’s north-west that were once considered a stronghold. In 2022, Labor’s primary vote in the seat fell by 17.8%, while its two-party-preferred vote dropped below 60% for the first time in three decades. The sitting MP, Natalie Hutchins, is retiring and her successor, Uros Rasic, has been campaigning since December. The party has been pouring in resources to defend its territory.

In neighbouring St Albans, Labor’s Natalie Suleyman’s primary vote fell by 18.4% at the last election. Farther north in Greenvale, there was a swing of almost 15% against Labor on a two-party preferred basis. In Yan Yean it was 11.3%. There are also fears for Victorian premier Ben Carroll’s seat of Niddrie, closer to the city.

These seats are among the most diverse in the state, and predominately working-to-middle class. Most households are paying off mortgages – meaning they’re exposed to rising interest rates.

Before the 2022 election, Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist turned pollster with Redbridge, warned this block of seats would swing away from the government in the wake of the Covid lockdowns. What has surprised him is how little Labor has done since to win these voters back.

“They clearly ignored it. They banked it, they thought that ‘it doesn’t matter how much we absorb out there, it doesn’t go to the Liberal party’. They just didn’t factor in that One Nation will be around to provide these people a home. So now here we are,” Samaras says.

“Is it going to result in lost seats? We’ll have to wait and see but I would not want to be in their shoes.”

Shopfront politics

Almost every storefront on Alfrieda Street in St Albans carries posters for one or even all four of the main candidates: Labor’s Natalie Suleyman, Liberal Rob Dunstan, One Nation’s John Cowell and Luan Walker of the West party. There are even a few posters for the Victorian Socialists but no visible Greens presence.

Jenny, who owns an Asian grocery store and has lived in the area for 20 years, has all four. She says her main concern this election is cost of living, as her business has suffered as customers cut back.

“The interest [rates are] too high for the customer, so they try to save money on fruit and veg,” she says.

She backs the sitting MP, Suleyman, to win, pointing to her visibility in the community.

“I don’t see them often,” she says of the other candidates whose faces fill her windows.

Several other traders say Suleyman, a former local mayor, has been responsive to their concerns, particularly around illegal trading on the strip, of everything from home-cooked meals to stolen meat and cosmetics.

Andy Nguyen, vice-president of the St Albans Asian Business Association, is campaigning heavily for Labor and says another party winning the seat will “never happen”. Suleyman gets back to him in “five minutes” when he raises his concerns, he says – or 10 minutes if she’s busy.

“That’s why my community, [the] Vietnamese community, support her.”

But others are more skeptical. Locals raise crime and drug use as high among their concerns. As students take their year 12 exams in the St Albans community centre, plastic baggies and syringes are littered across Errington Reserve.

TJ, a YouTuber who grew up in St Albans, says drug use is a “massive” problem in the area. “I’m not here to dis my home town but this is the reality.”

Another local, Sam, is most concerned about the firebombing of local storefronts as a result of the illicit tobacco trade. He is supportive of commitments from both One Nation and the Liberal party at a federal level to cut cigarette taxes in a bid to minimise the illegal trade – a commitment that has no bearing on state laws.

Shyam Padala, who lives in Melton, says the western suburbs have been “completely forgotten by Labor”, pointing to their promises to build a Melton hospital and electrify the train line – made in 2018 and then again in 2022 – which still haven’t eventuated.

He says it’s “cheating the ordinary middle class” to encourage people to move to the area on the promise better infrastructure, only to leave them waiting. The hospital, in particular, has become a running joke.

“It will never come. When we die it will come,” Padala says.

A ‘fresh face’

But could electorates such as St Albans – where almost two-thirds of the population have parents born overseas – turn to a party such as One Nation?

TJ remembers the anti-Asian rhetoric of the 1990s, when Pauline Hanson first rose to prominence, but says the perception of her has since shifted.

“Back then they looked at her as super-racist, but now they’re looking [at her] as a saviour. So it’s changed completely,” he says.

TJ says he’s not particularly political and is quick to acknowledge Labor’s achievements in the area – from the level crossing removals on the Sunbury line to the Joan Kirner Women’s and Children’s hospital. But he says as costs increase, it’s not enough.

“People are digging deeper into their pockets and they’ve got nothing left,” he says.

“They want change drastically and they don’t want the Liberals or Labor. They want a fresh face.

australia.title: One Nation asks donors at $3,000-a-head Sydney fundraiser to accept ‘non-disclosure agreement’
australia.snippet: Transparency experts raise concerns about plans to use NDA to gag attendees at event featuring Pauline Hanson in lead-up to NSW election ...
australia.content:
One Nation is attempting to gag donors from ever revealing details of discussions at an invite-only, cocktail-dress fundraiser with the party’s senior leadership team, in a move described as a “worrying precedent” for democracy.

Invitations to the “very special evening” at an undisclosed central Sydney venue next Thursday show donors will be charged $3,000 for a “private and very discrete” four-hour event.

Donors have been told they’ll meeting with Pauline Hanson; One Nation’s national director, James Ashby; federal MP Barnaby Joyce; the federal party’s chief of staff, Chris Taylor; and its New South Wales leader, Mike Newman.

But unlike at other One Nation fundraisers – including a $2,000 invite-only event in Melbourne in September – this time donors have been asked to abide by a “non-disclosure agreement” preventing them from disclosing the identities of any attendees. They are also stopped from sharing the nature of any discussions at the event, which is reportedly set to feature a “cocktail and canapé service throughout the evening as the sun sets” and a live auction.

“Do not disclose information about what occurs at the event, including conversations, activities, photographs, video or other details obtained through attending,” says the agreement, contained in an invitation seen by Guardian Australia.

“Do not provide information, photographs, recordings or comments about the event to journalists, media organisations, bloggers or other publishers.”

The NDA states that these obligations “continue after the event has concluded”.

These type of fundraising dinners are common and frequently organised by Labor and Liberal parties. But senior sources from both major parties involved in running such events say the use of non-disclosure agreements is unprecedented.

Transparency International Australia’s chief executive, Clancy Moore, has been a long-term critic of closed-door fundraising dinners and believes they offer “cash for access”. He said the use of non-disclosure agreements was a worrying new step.

“Charging guests for a political fundraiser and requiring them to keep quiet about it raises serious questions about transparency ahead of an important state election,” Moore said.

“Voters deserve to know whether any political commitments are being made behind closed doors to paying guests. A non-disclosure agreement should never be used to shield political fundraising from public scrutiny.”

Christian Slattery, a senior campaigner at the Australian Democracy Network, said Australians were “rightly suspicious of exclusive cash-for-access events”.

“Slapping an NDA on a political fundraiser sets a worrying precedent. Democracy thrives in the sunlight,” Slattery said.

One Nation has disclosed $5,000 in reportable donations so far in 2026-27, across three donations for a fundraising dinner with Joyce, according to disclosures with the NSW Electoral Commission.

In that time, disclosures indicate the NSW Labor party has raised $286,200 in total reportable donations, while the NSW Liberals have raised $95,900.

The individual threshold for a reportable donation in New South Wales is $1,000.

Major donations drive

A now-defunct webpage containing details of Thursday’s event had stated that registered attendees would receive a text message with its location just an hour before the start time.

In early September, the address of a three-course fundraising lunch with Hanson in Melbourne was leaked to the media, leading to journalists photographing donors as they entered the venue.

Other high-profile fundraisers in the state have been targeted by protesters, leading to clashes with One Nation supporters and a heavy police presence.

One Nation has also required candidates at state elections to sign non-disclosure agreements preventing them from discussing their potential candidacy with the media or revealing confidential information obtained during the process.

The fundraiser comes amid a major donations drive by the party in NSW, where it was polling at 25% of the first-preference vote, ahead of the Coalition on 24% and behind Labor on 29%, according to a Sydney Morning Herald Resolve poll in September. Polling conducted internally by Labor suggests One Nation could pick up more than 20 seats in the state’s lower house.

Newman and Joyce hosted several publicly advertised, small-ticket dinners and forums in October, with more events planned in November.

One Nation was contacted for comment.

world.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK
world.snippet: Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit A British healthcare ...
world.content:
A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.

“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”

The patient, whose identity is unknown, is in a stable condition and is expected to arrive in the UK on Wednesday or Thursday before being transferred in a specialist ambulance to a “high consequence” infectious disease unit, according to an official document seen by Reuters.

A humanitarian organisation sent the worker to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak.

The Royal Free hospital in London has a high-level isolation unit for infectious diseases such as Ebola; other centres are in Newcastle and Liverpool.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies.

The current outbreak, declared on 15 May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases, and 5,000 deaths. It is the 17th in DR Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus, and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history. The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way.

Since the outbreak started, it has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last month Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus. She, along with a close contact, were evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.

In an interview with the Guardian last month, Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said the “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak meant it could reach the UK and other countries.

“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said. “Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.

“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented.”

Other patients who have been medically evacuated for specialised care since the start of the outbreak include two sent to Germany and one to the Netherlands. Another case was reported in France in July.

British health authorities say the risk ⁠to the wider public from imported Ebola cases remains low and the NHS has procedures in place to manage suspected and confirmed infections.

There have only been four confirmed cases recorded in Britain since 1976, ‌according to the UK Health Security Agency.

world.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections
world.snippet: Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts The African National Congress is o...
world.content:
The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.

The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.

In Kensington, a diverse Johannesburg suburb that has sustained repeated water and power outages in recent weeks, voters said they wanted to see change. The city is currently led by Dada Morero, the ANC mayor, in coalition with the far-left Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) and the rightwing populist Patriotic Alliance (PA).

“Service delivery is bad, it’s horrible,” said Tshepiso Makotse, 26, a call centre worker. “Water, electricity – everything, basically.”

Makotse said she had split her two votes, casting one for the centre-right Democratic Alliance (DA) local councillor and her party vote for the leftwing uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma. “I just want change,” she said.

Terrence Pieters, a retired boilermaker, said: “The infrastructure in Johannesburg is shot.” He declined to say which party he had voted for, other than it was “one of the offshoots of the DA”.

“I would like to see things get better and great people in charge,” said the 72-year-old. “But … there’s no one party that’s going to take over here. It’s going to be a circus, it’s going to be a coalition.”

Vote fragmentation means the ANC could still end up leading many city coalition governments while losing control of others.

Unstable coalitions are already a feature of many of South Africa’s 257 municipalities, and analysts point to their high turnover as a major reason for poor service delivery.

Johannesburg, a city of 4.8 million people that has faced water shortages for more than a week, has had 10 mayors in as many years. The neighbouring municipality of Ekurhuleni has had three mayors since 2021. To the north, in Tshwane, which contains the capital, Pretoria, the mayoralty has rotated between parties four times since 2020. In October, more than 800 people contracted a gastrointestinal illness from contaminated water in Bronkhorstspruit, in east Tshwane.

The ANC’s national leadership is open to working with the DA in Gauteng, according to South African media, mirroring the government of national unity, where the two parties are the largest in the national coalition. However, local ANC leaders are reportedly not in favour of a DA tie-up. Currently, the ANC governs in various coalitions across the province’s three metros, including under an ActionSA mayor in Tshwane.

In Johannesburg, the DA’s Helen Zille has led a spirited campaign, with viral stunts including the 75-year-old snorkelling in a pothole and kayaking along a flooded street. However, the former Cape Town mayor is still viewed with suspicion by many, especially black voters, due to past comments appearing to excuse colonialism. Some voters also point to soaring housing costs in Cape Town, which has been run by the DA since 2006, as a reason not to vote for Zille.

The former Johannesburg DA mayor Herman Mashaba, who now leads ActionSA, which is polling around 10%, has ruled out working with Zille in Johannesburg. Mashaba has called Zille a “racist”, an allegation she has always fervently denied. The ANC, for its part, has three possible mayoral candidates for the city, amid factional infighting.

In eThekwini metro, which contains the port city of Durban, the MK party was polling above 40%. Zuma, its 84-year-old leader, who has weathered and denied numerous corruption allegations, is set to take many of the votes of his former party, which won 42% in eThekwini in 2021 and is now polling around 10%.

The DA looks set to retain its majority in Cape Town, although probably with less than the 58% of the vote it won in 2021, as unaffordable housing turns more voters against the party.

South Africa’s electoral commission will have a week to announce the final results of Wednesday’s vote, which chooses councillors and parties, with mayors not directly elected. Parties will then have two weeks from the announcement to form councils and elect mayors.

world.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
world.snippet: There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective Cora Bailey has been encountering ill...
world.content:
Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.

South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.

Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.

The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.

The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.

However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.

“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.

“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

world.title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
world.snippet: Critics cite Lana Nusseibeh’s denial of accusations the UAE is fuelling Sudan war by supporting paramilitary RSF Members of the Sudanese ...
world.content:
Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.

Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.

There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”

He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.

“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”

Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

world.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
world.snippet: Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website Lina Attalah,...
world.content:
Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.

Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”
